subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: The unit teaches four connected ideas. First, what a database is, and the difference between a physical and a digital database. Second, that every database is built from records and fields — each record is all the data about one thing (one row), and each field is one piece of data (one column, with a heading). Fourth, how to collect data with a form, how to search a database to find records, and how to sort data into ascending and descending order.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 4 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Say what a database is (an organised collection of related data) and give examples.
Tell the difference between a physical (paper) and a digital (computer) database, and give one advantage of each.
Name the parts of a database: a record (one row — all the data about one thing) and a field (one column, with a heading).
Explain the difference between data (raw facts) and information (processed data that has meaning).
Give some advantages and disadvantages of using a form to collect data.
Search a small database to find the records that match.
Sort data into ascending (A-Z, small to large) and descending (Z-A, large to small) order, by hand and in a spreadsheet.

concepts.title: What is a database? Physical and digital
concepts.explanation:
A database is an organised collection of related data. A phone's contact list is a database. A database can be physical (kept on paper) or digital (kept on a computer). Every database is made of records and fields: each record is all the data about one thing (one row), and each field is one piece of data (one column, with a heading).

Imagine the teacher at Ehel Academy writes each pupil's details on a sheet of paper and keeps every sheet in a filing cabinet. That is a physical database — it is on paper. It works, but searching for one pupil takes time, changing a sheet is messy, and it needs a lot of space. Now imagine the same details are typed into the computer.
concepts.example: That is a digital database. It fits on a tiny storage device, it is quick to search, and it is easy to change and to sort.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you sort examples into physical and digital, and point to one record and one field on a card?

concepts.title: Data and information
concepts.explanation:
Information is what we get after the data has been processed, sorted and given meaning. Data answers “what are the facts?” ; information answers “so what do the facts tell us?”

What do these numbers mean? Now add the missing meaning: “These are the numbers of books six pupils in the reading club read this term.” Suddenly we can work things out: Maya read the most (20 books), Sana read the fewest (7), and the club read 74 books in total. Those useful facts are information — the data has been processed.
concepts.example: Find one real example of data and information around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you tell that a plain list of facts is data, while a sentence that tells us something useful (the most, the fewest, the total) is information? Watch for you who thinks any number is automatically information.

concepts.title: Using forms to collect data
concepts.explanation:
Before we can store data in a database, we have to collect it. A form is a document with headings and spaces used to collect data. A form can be paper-based or electronic (on a computer or phone). Forms are useful, but they also have some drawbacks.

Do you have a library card? Yes / No.
concepts.example: Because everyone fills in the same headings, all the answers come back in the same shape. That makes it easy to type them into our database and easy to compare.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that a form is for collecting data, while a database is for storing it — you are not the same thing. Can you give at least one advantage and one disadvantage of using a form?

concepts.title: Searching and sorting (unplugged)
concepts.explanation:
Two of the most useful things a data controller does are search and sort. To sort is to put the records in order. Ascending order goes from smallest to largest, or A to Z. Descending order goes from largest to smallest, or Z to A.

First search: say “Show me every pupil whose favourite subject is Science,” and you can pull out the matching cards. When they reach Sami and Sana, stop and teach the letter-by-letter rule. Use the six index cards from Session 1.
concepts.example: Find one real example of searching and sorting around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you sort words A-Z using the letter-by-letter rule, and sort numbers both ways? Can you search by hand to find matching records? Watch for you who sorts words by length instead of by letters.

concepts.title: Sort a database on the computer
concepts.explanation:
In this session you type the reading-club database into a free spreadsheet and use the Sort button. This shows why a digital database is so much faster to sort than a paper one.

Type the headings in the first row and the six records underneath. Watch — by hand this took us a few minutes. The computer will do it in one second.
concepts.example: Open LibreOffice Calc (or any spreadsheet). Explain that a spreadsheet is a grid of rows and columns, and each little box is a cell.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you choose the field to sort by and pick ascending or descending? Can you notice that each record stays together as a whole row? Can you type the data into the right cells, highlight the whole table, and use Data then Sort?

esafety.title: Keep personal information private
esafety.text: Your full name, address, school, phone number, birthday and passwords are personal information. Never type them into a game, an app or a website, and never send them to someone you only know online.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Write one advantage and one disadvantage of using a form.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A disadvantage of an electronic form: you need a device to fill it in (accept: private data must be kept safe, or it can cost to set up).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Put these names in ascending order: Karim, Grace, Maya, Sami.
Put these numbers in descending order: 15, 7, 20, 11.
Explain the key idea in searching and sorting (unplugged), and give one example of your own.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
Two of the most useful things a data controller does are search and sort. To sort is to put the records in order. Ascending order goes from smallest to largest, or A to Z. Descending order goes from largest to smallest, or Z to A.

First search: say “Show me every pupil whose favourite subject is Science,” and you can pull out the matching cards. When they reach Sami and Sana, stop and teach the letter-by-letter rule. Use the six index cards from Session 1.

project.title: Unit 2 Project: Be a Data Controller
project.brief: Bring together everything from Be a Data Controller into one finished piece of work you can show and explain.
steps: Plan first: write down what your be a data controller project has to do before you build anything.
Build the smallest version that does one of those things, and run it.
Add one feature at a time, testing after each one.
When something breaks, change one thing, run it again, and note what fixed it.
Check your work against every success criterion below before you call it finished.
successCriteria: I made five cards with the same three fields.
I wrote one record on each card.
I sorted the cards by Name (A to Z) and by Age (oldest first).
I typed the same database into a spreadsheet.
I sorted it with Data then Sort.
I wrote one piece of information from my data.

selfAssessment: I can say what a database is (an organised collection of related data) and give examples.
I can tell the difference between a physical (paper) and a digital (computer) database, and give one advantage of each.
I can name the parts of a database: a record (one row — all the data about one thing) and a field (one column, with a heading).
I can explain the difference between data (raw facts) and information (processed data that has meaning).
I can give some advantages and disadvantages of using a form to collect data.
I can search a small database to find the records that match.
I can sort data into ascending (A-Z, small to large) and descending (Z-A, large to small) order, by hand and in a spreadsheet.
